newsitem.title: USA: HMOs help change role of hospitals -- U.S. study.
newsitem.headline: HMOs help change role of hospitals -- U.S. study.

text.p: Health maintenance organisations (HMOs) are helping to change the role of the hospital in the American health care system, a researcher said Tuesday.

HMOs have shifted hospitals away from the centre of the health care system and have also reduced growth of hospital spending in areas of high HMO penetration in California, James Robinson, of the University of California, Berkeley's School of Public Health, said.
HMOs, which have grown quickly in United States in recent years, provide health care through a network of doctors and hospitals. Patients pay a fixed co-payment for services.
"We are witnessing an historic transformation in the role of the hospital within the American health care delivery system," Robinson said.

At the start of this century, most medical services were delivered in the doctor's office or the patient's home and the hospital was a health care provider of last resort. Over time, hospitals became increasingly important.

"Now, 100 years later, the pendulum is swinging back the other way," Robinson said. Technological advances permit many medical and surgical procedures that had required in-patient facilities to be performed in the surgery, doctor's office, nursing facility or a patient's home, he said.
Robinson's findings were published in The Journal of the American Medical Association and presented at the association's science reporters conference here.
By studying data on California hospitals, Robinson found that hospital spending grew 44 percent less rapidly in markets with high HMO penetration than in markets with low HMO penetration.
"Managed care is shifting the acute care hospital from the centre toward the periphery of the care system," he said.

In California, HMOs "are continuing to push down on hospital utilization, both through fewer admissions and shorter lengths of stay, thereby achieving the lowest rate of hospital use in the nation," Robinson said.

Statistics from 1983 to 1993 show that acute care hospital discharges dropped by 15 percent, the average length of hospital stays fell by 19 percent and the number of in-patient days per hospital dropped by 29 percent in markets with low HMO penetration. But in markets with high HMO penetration, they declined by 23 percent, 20 percent and 44 percent respectively, the study found.
